one_liner: Pure C API (list, set, map, queue, stack, string, bitmap) wrapping libstdc++ containers; matches libstdc++ at best, never beats it.
what_it_does: libcdada gives C programs std::list, std::set, std::map, std::queue, std::stack and std::string behind opaque handles and void* functions (cdada_set_create(uint32_t), cdada_set_insert(set, &key), cdada_list_push_back, cdada_map_insert(map, &key, val_ptr)). Keys and list values are copied by value; map values are stored only as void* pointers that the caller owns. It is not a faster container: the README promises performance 'comparable to libstdc++', and the benchmark doc measures wrapper overhead.
how_it_is_fast: It adds no new algorithm: every call dispatches through a switch on key size to a pre-instantiated std::set/std::map/std::list of uint8/16/32/64_t or a padded 16-256 byte POD (compared with memcmp). Default containers round keys up to the next power of two (memset plus memcpy into a padded temporary on every call); 'custom containers' (CDADA_*_CUSTOM_GEN macros or the cdada-gen script) instantiate the libstdc++ container for your exact struct type in a small C++ file, removing the padding cost.
when_to_use: C code bases (network daemons such as pmacct, which builds libcdada in-tree per issue #7) that want tested ordered set/map/list containers without writing a red-black tree
Fixed-size POD keys whose size is 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, where the default containers run close to native libstdc++ (uint32 set insert 746 vs 752 ticks)

Larger or odd-sized structs (for example 69 or 444 bytes) if you add a custom-container C++ file, which keeps set rows within 2 percent of native and list rows within 3 ticks (69-byte list pop_back 25 vs 22)
Single-threaded, Linux/POSIX user-space code that already links libstdc++
when_not_to_use: You want something faster than the STL: it is the STL plus a call, a switch and a key copy; plf::list or ankerl::svector are the entries that actually beat std containers

Erase-heavy map workloads: cdada_map_erase does find() and then erase(key), a second tree lookup, so map erase runs 1.37-1.54x slower than native (1009 vs 722 ticks uint32, 1768 vs 1148 for 69-byte keys, 2021 vs 1472 for 444-byte custom)
You need a hash table: despite the README's 'hashmap' wording, cdada_map is std::map (O(log n), ordered); wrapping std::unordered_map is still an open feature request (#13)
Concurrent access (README: not thread-safe), keys over 256 bytes without custom containers, or variable-length string keys (open request #12)
Non-x86 or non-glibc toolchains with -Werror: configure forces -Werror, and an OpenWrt ARM g++ build fails on a memcpy overflow warning in __list_internal.h (open issue #14)

integration.dependencies: libstdc++ (C++98); autotools (autoconf, automake, libtool) to build; python3 only for the cdada-gen custom-container generator
integration.min_toolchain: C (gnu89) plus any gcc-compatible C++98 compiler (gcc, clang, icc per README)
integration.platforms: POSIX (Linux tested; a FreeBSD build error inside pmacct was fixed in closed issue #7); Windows not supported; the benchmark's RDTSC timer is x86-only and prints zeros elsewhere
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same libstdc++ containers underneath, but a C void* API with E_EXISTS/E_NOT_FOUND return codes instead of templates and iterators; C++ code gains nothing by switching

gotchas: Harness and code finding: the std::set/std::map baseline in test/benchmark.cc is written to mirror cdada's own insert pattern (find(), then insert(it, k) with it == end()), which for the 500,000 shuffled keys in array.s3 is a wrong hint and triggers a second full tree descent; idiomatic set.insert(k) or lower_bound plus hinted insert does one descent, so the 'comparable to libstdc++' parity is against a baseline slowed to cdada's double-lookup pattern, and real overhead versus idiomatic C++ code is larger than the table shows.

Map erase is the one row where the baseline does not mirror the library: the baseline erases by iterator, while cdada_map_erase_u (also used by custom maps) calls find() and then erase(*key), a redundant second lookup; switching to erase(it) is a one-line fix that would likely remove the 1.4x map-erase gap.

Default containers pad keys to a power of two and order them by memcmp of the padded bytes, so traversal order of struct keys is byte-wise little-endian rather than numeric, and non-power-of-two keys pay a memset plus memcpy per call (69-byte list pop_back 40 vs 22 ticks).
Positional access is linear: cdada_list_get and cdada_set_get_pos walk the container with std::advance (O(n)), as std::list would.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libcdada only when the caller must be C: every sibling in this category (plf::list, plf::colony, plf::stack, ankerl::svector, veque, fast_vector, EASTL vector) is a C++ template that actually beats the std container, while libcdada at best ties libstdc++. From C++ code, use std containers or those siblings directly.
verified_claims_summary: doc/Benchmarks.md times 500,000 unique shuffled uint32 keys (also inside 69- and 444-byte packed structs), inserted then erased, 10 repetitions, averaged RDTSC ticks per op at -O3 against libstdc++ from Debian 10 on an Intel Core i7-8565U (compiler version unstated, one run, no variance). libcdada ties native on uint32 set/map insert (746 vs 752, 809 vs 830) and on custom containers for large structs, and is slower on map erase (about 1.4x), list push_back (28 vs 20) and padded 69-byte lists (67 vs 42, 40 vs 22); there is no speedup.
status_note: Maintained by a single author (v0.6.4 bug-fix release on 2026-02-27, last commit 2026-03-01, 30 stars, BSD-2-Clause) and small enough to vendor, but it is a convenience C wrapper, not a performance win, and four feature/bug issues (#12, #13, #14, #21) remain open.
